title: Middle East watch
dek: One war, three fronts: Iran's sanctioned exports under the naval blockade, tanker movement through the Strait of Hormuz, and Houthi pressure on Red Sea shipping. The fronts move together; this page tracks them together. Every number is either tracker-observed or claimed, never both; bullets say which. When any front tightens, buyers bid up substitute sours and the whole complex firms, supporting Canadian differentials; when they loosen, medium and heavy sours soften.

claims.text: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Oct 30 that two oil tankers were involved in incidents and stopped in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring radio warnings and attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway, Reuters reported. Iran also said on Oct 30 that it destroyed a US unmanned vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the US military.

A small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Oct 29, causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel, in the first successful use of such explosives in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February, maritime sources told Reuters on Oct 30. The tanker was the Panama-flagged Louise 1, according to assessments from three maritime security sources. The crew was safe, there was no environmental impact and the fire had been extinguished, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said, adding that the vessel, which it did not name, was continuing to its next port of call. The incident occurred 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, UKMTO said, and it was not immediately clear who was behind the attack. Greece-based maritime risk group Marisks said the apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the strait's congested shipping lanes. Ukrainian forces also hit the Louise 1 in July with naval drones in the Black Sea over what Ukraine's SBU security service said was its role in transporting Russian oil as part of the shadow fleet.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Oct 29 that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines while attempting to cross an unauthorised route south of the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours, in a statement shared by state media, Reuters reported. The tankers had switched off their radar and navigation systems and ignored warnings from the Guards' navy, which said the vessels had been abandoned on the southern shores of the strait. No vessel names, flags or casualty details were given, and the claim had not been independently confirmed.

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Oct 29 that it had received a report of an incident in the Strait of Hormuz, 9 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, where the master of a third-party vessel reported sighting another vessel on fire. The status of the crew is unknown, and there is no damage assessment or environmental impact report at present, UKMTO said. UKMTO advised vessels transiting the area to proceed with caution and report any suspicious activity. Whether the burning vessel is one of the three tankers in the IRGC mine claim reported the same day had not been established.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards the kingdom's eastern region early on Oct 29, Reuters reported, as hostilities between the two sides showed no signs of abating. Yemeni government forces said the Houthis attacked Aden airport on Oct 28. The attacks came a day after the Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, with a missile, a strike Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm.

Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters on Oct 28, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer. The proposal sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran's and Washington's concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps each side must take, and the timeline could begin early next week with several countries acting as guarantors, the briefed official said. The senior Iranian official said Tehran's policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged. Washington wants Iran's nuclear programme to be part of negotiations from the outset, while Iran says its conditions, which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports, must be met first.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct 27 that they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile, Reuters reported. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the strike caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and sits on the Gulf west of the Strait of Hormuz, and Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Ras Tanura has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure. The Houthis also said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait, and had repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, with no immediate Saudi confirmation of those attacks either. The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh, and civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the capital on Tuesday afternoon.

Iran's navy said on Oct 27 that an oil tanker caught fire after striking naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, accusing the vessel of entering a prohibited area with its tracking systems switched off, state media reported, in a Reuters report carried by Devdiscourse. The Iranian army statement, carried by the official IRNA news agency, said the tanker had attempted to cross a prohibited and dangerous area east of the strait. No vessel name, flag or casualty details were given in the reporting, and the claim had not been independently confirmed. Iran has reported on multiple occasions that tankers struck naval mines while attempting to transit areas Tehran considers off-limits, and tracker and maritime-security reporting earlier in October found no credible evidence for several of those earlier mine claims.

Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body set up by Tehran to manage passage requests in the Strait of Hormuz, said on Oct 27 that all vessels belonging to South Korean shipping company Sinokor would face legal action starting on November 1, Reuters reported. The authority said on X that Sinokor vessels had committed the highest number of crossing violations in the strait over the past three months, and that appropriate actions had been taken against at least seven of them. Sinokor did not immediately comment. Ships owned by Sinokor were previously included on a list issued by Iran in August of 45 tankers that it said had broken its rules for crossing the strait. Reuters noted that Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on shipping by relying on so-called dark transits, switching off tankers' tracking systems to evade detection, while the US naval blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Oct 27 that it intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles and drones launched by the Houthis towards two regions of Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported. The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles towards Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region, and four drones towards the country's Southern Region, the coalition said. Saudi Civil Defense issued early warning alerts for a potential hostile threat in the Eastern Region and in Kharj governorate, later saying the danger had passed in both areas. Saudi Arabia has intensified its strikes on the Houthis since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted attacks between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis.

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued a time-late report on Oct 26 of a strike on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Oct 23, as reports spread of a vessel on fire off Basra, Iraq, in the north of the Arabian Gulf, Seatrade Maritime News reported. The UKMTO report said an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile at 0839 on Oct 23 and that the crew were reported safe. Maritime security company Orbital Risk Intelligence reported that a vessel had been attacked off Basra on Oct 26 and was on fire, and a NASA satellite confirmed heat emitting from the area at 0926 hrs. UKMTO said earlier this month that it was struggling with shipowners' refusal to report incidents, and that the majority of incidents were not being reported to it. Over the weekend, Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority updated its non-compliance list with two additional vessels, the Liberian-flagged VLCC Senegal Prosperity, owned by Sinokor, and the Panama-flagged LPG tanker Sea Soar; the list now contains 123 vessels.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct 26 that they had attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pumping stations and Riyadh airport, Reuters reported. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said earlier it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the capital Sanaa, including one used to fire a missile towards Riyadh that the coalition said it had intercepted. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. The Houthis also said they had struck Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after an attack claimed by the group earlier this month killed 13 people. The Houthis also said on Saturday they had targeted the East-West pipeline, crude oil pumping stations, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the Rabigh refinery, and there was no Saudi confirmation of those claims either. The Saudi coalition said on Monday it had also carried out a military operation against Houthi targets in Yemen, destroying five tunnels used to store ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and a missile storage facility.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Oct 25 that in recent months over 95 percent of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz have sailed through safely despite aggression by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Anadolu Agency reported via MCI Group. CENTCOM said American troops had reached the milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer, and that American forces have assisted more than 3,000 merchant vessels in navigating the chokepoint over the past six months, noting that momentum expanded after the US dismantled naval mines deployed across international sea lanes by the IRGC. CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper visited the waterway on Oct 25, flying over the strait.
claims.source: MCI Group (citing CENTCOM via Anadolu Agency)

claims.text: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct 24 that they had launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports, and the Saudi-led coalition said it had downed two missiles, Reuters reported. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline, as well as King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif, and Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles fell in the Mecca and Medina regions and in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi claims, and it was not immediately clear whether any of the reported attacks had hit their targets or had been intercepted. Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern port city of Aden.

President Donald Trump accused Iran on Oct 22 of fabricating tanker incidents to drive up oil prices ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections, writing on Truth Social that Iran was doing everything it could to drive up the price of oil and was making up fake hits, mines and everything else, and claiming more oil was coming through the Strait of Hormuz than before the conflict began. The accusation is a political claim, not independent verification that the reported incidents were fabricated, and confirmed attacks on Saudi territory and maritime security concerns continue to support the risk premium in crude futures.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) office received a time-late report on Oct 23 of a tanker hit by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz on Oct 22 at 5:15 p.m. UTC, 7 nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman, UKMTO said in Warning 181-26. The tanker was able to continue its voyage to the next port of call. UKMTO has also told the shipping site gCaptain that many targeted ships do not report to it, so a missing report does not prove nothing happened.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said on Oct 23 that two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil struck naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, a claim compiled by NewsPlainly on Oct 24 from reports by Anadolu, Euronews, gCaptain, Iran International, Al Jazeera and Tasnim. None of the ships said to have hit mines has been named, and the Oct 23 claim was not confirmed by anyone, NewsPlainly said. The statement is the latest in a series of October mine claims: the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) found no substantiation for an Oct 17 claim, UKMTO logged one incident with no damage reported for Oct 19-20, and US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the mine claims for Oct 21-22 were incorrect.

An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates, prompting containment operations and environmental assessments, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Oct 23, Reuters reported. All beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments, fishermen and other sea users were urged to avoid affected areas, and the ministry said odours reported by residents in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain posed no health risks. The ministry did not say what caused the spill, and authorities had not identified the tanker involved.

All 14 Indian nationals on a yacht involved in an incident off Yemen's coast are reported safe and located around Hodeidah, the Indian embassy in Yemen said on Oct 23, Reuters reported. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct 22 that they were rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack. Saudi authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on Oct 22. The embassy said it would continue to work for the well-being of the nationals, and India's foreign ministry said on Oct 22 that it condemned the attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on Oct 22, six people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensified. Staff were instructed to evacuate the building and work remotely, following a wave of Houthi attacks targeting the company and Saudi airports, in what would be the first headquarters evacuation since the start of the Iran war. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the reason for the evacuation was unclear, and Saudi Arabia's benchmark index dropped 2.5 percent on Oct 22 following the news, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had launched attacks on Aramco facilities in Yanbu and the Saudi defence ministry in Riyadh, which Saudi authorities did not confirm, and the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted drones over Riyadh and Medina.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Oct 22 that four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Oct 21, and that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported. The IRGC warned the US military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. The claims had not been independently confirmed in the Reuters report.

The US State Department ordered non-emergency US government employees and their family members to depart its missions in Saudi Arabia on Oct 21, Reuters reported, as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the department ordered the departure in Saudi Arabia only amid attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets. Four US officials told Reuters that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave, which Pigott did not address.

Yemen's Houthi forces claimed on Oct 22 that they launched a rescue operation after Saudi Arabia allegedly targeted an Indian yacht carrying 14 Indian nationals near Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said. The Houthis characterised the alleged strike as a threat to international navigation in the Red Sea. No independent verification of the claim was immediately available.

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Oct 21 that an unknown projectile struck a tanker 11 nautical miles west of Bukha, Oman, which overlooks the Strait of Hormuz, at about 0145 GMT. A fire that erupted was extinguished, the tanker was at anchor, and all crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact reported, Reuters reported the same day.

UKMTO also reported that an unidentified projectile struck a tanker about 30 nautical miles southeast of Al Faw port, Iraq, on Oct 20, with all crew safe and no damage or environmental impact reported. An Iraqi source told Shafaq News on Oct 21 that Iraq had not yet confirmed the reported strike occurred within Iraqi territorial waters.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Oct 20 that two tankers that violated its navigation rules struck naval mines laid in the southern transit zone of the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire and halted, and warned that oil companies would pay a higher price if US actions continue. The IRGC did not name the vessels and the claim had not been independently confirmed. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) separately reported an incident involving a tanker and military personnel about 121 nautical miles east of Duqm, Oman, with military personnel approaching the tanker as part of ongoing military activity in the region. Attacks on merchant ships in the strait have intensified, with at least 18 vessels attacked over the past two weeks, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler.

UKMTO is struggling to accurately report the true number of attacks on shipping in the region because the majority of attacked vessels are refusing to report to the Royal Navy-linked organisation, Seatrade Maritime reported on Oct 19, citing UKMTO's latest weekly update published Oct 16. Since that update, UKMTO has reported four more attacks in the Arabian Gulf, the Gulf of Aden and the Strait of Hormuz. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) has raised its threat level in the Arabian Gulf to substantial from moderate, citing increased Iranian attacks since Oct 7 and increased navigational interference, and said there is no substantiation to the IRGC Navy's weekend claims that two supertankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. UKMTO has issued 29 warnings on 28 incidents in October to date, with 153 incidents reported since Mar 1, 2026.

UKMTO reported on Oct 18 that a tug travelling southbound northeast of Khor Fakkan, on the UAE's Gulf of Oman coast, was struck by two unknown projectiles, damaging the vessel, which continued on its route, with one person suffering a minor injury. UKMTO did not name the tug, its flag or its operator, and did not identify an attacker.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 17 that a second supertanker, also carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude, was engulfed in a massive blaze after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz hours after the first and was left immobilised, IRNA reported. Both vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and used a route Iran had not authorised, and one tried to cross with US support, the Guards said; no vessel names were given and Reuters reported there was no independent confirmation of either incident. Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera showed oil flows through the strait fell from 20.8 million barrels on Oct 8 to 2.9 million barrels on Oct 11.

UKMTO reported that an LNG tanker 140 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla, Yemen, was fired on at 10:30 UTC on Oct 17 by a small skiff carrying seven people; the tanker's armed security team fired two warning shots in response and the skiff changed course. UKMTO did not identify the tanker and reported no boarding.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 17 that an oil tanker carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil exploded and caught fire after hitting a naval mine while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media reported. The Guards said the tanker was attempting to transit the strategic waterway through a route unauthorised by Iran. No vessel name was given in the report.

UKMTO reported late on Oct 16 that at least 12 ships were attacked in the week ending Oct 16, the highest monthly pace of ship attacks since the war began on Feb 28, and warned it is struggling to report the true number because most attacked vessels refuse to report. Of the 12 confirmed attacks, half the vessels continued to their destination or reached port, one sank, two were disabled, and three were damaged or had an unconfirmed outcome. UKMTO also reported a tanker hit on Oct 17 by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat 78 nautical miles northeast of Jubail, Saudi Arabia, damaging its aft port quarter.

US Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Oct 16 that Iran has no exports and no imports by sea, apart from humanitarian assistance allowed in, and that US forces have prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil in recent months. Cooper said about 400 merchant ships transited the Strait of Hormuz over the previous seven days and US forces had assisted Gulf partners in moving more than 100 million barrels of crude through the waterway in that period, adding that the strait is controlled by the United States and its regional partners, not Iran.

Ship attack reports in and around the Strait of Hormuz hit a record high, BBC Verify reported on Oct 16 from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) data: 12 vessels were attacked between Oct 5 and Oct 11, the largest weekly total since the US-Israeli war with Iran began, after 10 the previous week, with six struck on a single Sunday and four more reported so far this week. The recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen in September has slowed as the strikes rose.

Kpler data reported on Oct 16 put oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz at a daily average of 11.62 million b/d in the week to Oct 13, down from a baseline of 17.15 million b/d, as Iranian strikes on tankers cut transits. Oil was on course for a weekly gain, with Brent at $105.48 and WTI at $97.40 on Oct 16, and ING said the market is pricing a significant Hormuz risk premium that would only fully unwind with a US-Iran agreement.

Yemen's Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in Aden on Oct 15, killing five people, the Yemeni government said, in the first attack on the Al-Maashiq palace in the current conflict. The Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in recent weeks, and government forces said last week they had recovered ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Iran's army said on Oct 15 that a violating oil tanker was on fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz after disabling its tracking systems and trying to pass through a restricted area in the Gulf of Oman, according to a statement carried by state media.

Oil fell more than 1 percent on Oct 15, with Brent down $1.64 to $104.42 and WTI down 98 cents to $94.11 by 0337 GMT, as traders weighed Hormuz shipping attacks against a US official saying Washington is considering easing sanctions on shadow-fleet vessels to cut shipping costs and let legal oil flow on previously sanctioned ships.

Two Singapore-registered container ships were struck by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Oct 13 and Oct 14, Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said. GFS Pride caught fire and sank, with all 21 crew evacuated safely; GFS Giselle took hull damage, reached a safe anchorage under its own power, and all 22 crew were safe.

Iranian officials told Reuters on Oct 14 that Tehran began using different offensive tactics about 10 days ago against vessels it deems in violation of its Hormuz restrictions, aiming to keep oil prices high. UKMTO said a container ship and a tanker were hit by unknown projectiles in the strait on Oct 13, and Iran's IRGC Navy said a container ship sank south of the strait after hitting a naval mine and catching fire. Brent was up 14 cents to $105.83 and WTI up 57 cents to $94.71 by 0938 GMT on Oct 14.

Iran's IRGC Navy said on Oct 12 that a third tanker in two days had struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz after using an unauthorized route with its navigation system switched off, and warned that vessels cooperating with US forces or transiting with identification systems off will face a decisive response. The claim named a shuttle tanker carrying about 750,000 barrels; no vessel name was given in the statement.

The US military disabled the Panama-flagged bulk carrier M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, in the Gulf of Oman on Oct 10 after the vessel departed an Iranian port and ignored repeated warnings to turn back. A US fighter jet struck the stern with a precision munition, fully disabling propulsion with no crew injuries, per US Central Command.

A drone struck the Nicaragua-flagged tanker MT Petro Dolphin at Sohar Anchorage off Oman on Oct 11, leaving two Indian seafarers missing and nine rescued, according to India's shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal. UKMTO confirmed the vessel was hit by a drone and reclassified the incident as an attack.

India's Ministry of External Affairs condemned attacks on two tankers in the Hormuz region on Oct 11, including the Marshall Islands-flagged MT Valthera, which was hit by an unknown projectile and caught fire. All 11 Indian seafarers aboard Valthera were reported safe after the fire was brought under control. No group had claimed responsibility for either attack in initial reporting.

UKMTO reported an outbound tanker struck on the port side by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz at 19:20 UTC on Oct 10, starting a fire on board; the crew was reported safe and vessels were advised to transit with caution. Separately the same day, masters near Ras Al Khaimah reported VHF broadcasts directing them to move from their anchorages.

The UAE National Guard's Coast Guard rescued 22 crew members from an oil tanker that caught fire in the Arabian Gulf, all reported in stable condition; Arab News linked the rescue to the same weekend as the Oct 9 strike on the Panama-flagged supertanker GEM NO.2 off the UAE coast, though reports did not confirm it was the same vessel.

UKMTO said a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, on Friday, with a fire later extinguished; maritime security sources identified it as the Panama-flagged crude supertanker GEM NO.2, fully laden at anchor, and said the strike outside the Hormuz area signaled widening tanker risk.

The US Treasury imposed fresh Iran sanctions on Oct 8 under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' designating 17 tankers plus individuals and networks moving Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals. Treasury officials said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude and has only about 20 million barrels left on vessels outside the blockade.

Kpler data showed crude crossing the Strait of Hormuz fell 27% week over week to about 10.1 million b/d on Oct 8, with only seven commodity carriers transiting on Tuesday, the lowest since late July, as fresh Iranian tanker strikes and record Persian Gulf freight rates tightened vessel supply.

Oil prices rose on Oct 30 and were on track for a fourth monthly gain as traders braced for a potential escalation in the US-Iran conflict after the US midterm elections, with an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz highlighting supply risks from the war, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures for December, which expire on Oct 30, were up $2.74, or 2.4 percent, at $117.62 a barrel as of 1045 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate crude climbed $2.18, or 2.1 percent, to $104.18; for the month, Brent was on course to finish close to 14 percent higher and WTI about 15 percent higher. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Oct 30 as part of coordinated efforts to reach a deal between the US and Iran, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters. On Oct 29, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including its largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility in Abqaiq owned by Saudi Aramco, and a Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region. President Trump said on Oct 29 that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country get medical supplies, after US media reported Vance had written to Tehran's top security official to revive peace talks; Iran has received the letter but has not responded yet, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported. ExxonMobil and Chevron have cancelled plans for their executives to travel to the United Arab Emirates' biggest oil show next week, two sources told Reuters.

Oil prices fell on Oct 29, paring gains made a day earlier, as hopes for peace talks took the edge off renewed concerns over Middle East supply disruptions, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures declined $1.22, or 1.1 percent, to $114.10 a barrel at 0351 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.33, or 1.3 percent, at $101.45. Brent rose 1.3 percent and WTI gained 3 percent on Oct 28. US Vice President JD Vance sought to revive peace negotiations by sending a letter to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei, the Wall Street Journal said on Oct 28, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter. Yuki Takashima, an economist at Nomura Securities, said selling pressure was prevailing amid expectations that peace talks may resume, but the decline remained limited due to concerns over intensified Houthi attacks and fears the US may launch an attack on Iran following its midterm elections on November 3. Iran's foreign minister said on Oct 28 that Tehran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed.

Oil prices rose by more than $2 on Oct 28 after an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude exporter, renewed concerns about supply risks, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures rose $2.02, or 1.8 percent, to $115.90 a barrel as of 0735 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $2.01, or 2.0 percent, at $101.91. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a missile, and Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike on the 550,000 barrel-per-day facility. Prices had dropped nearly $2 on Tuesday before swinging higher. ING commodity strategists said the market is still pricing in a greater likelihood of re-escalation, that oil prices remain elevated as the market waits for greater clarity on President Trump's next move toward Iran, and that if the market gets past the US elections without renewed strikes on Iran, that might be enough for the risk premium to start eroding.

Crude prices retreated on Oct 27, with NYMEX WTI crude for December delivery falling $1.86, or 1.83 percent, to settle at $99.90 a barrel, after rising to $102.82 during the session, and ICE Brent for December delivery closing down $1.93, or 1.7 percent, at $113.88 a barrel, DTN reported. Traders weighed diplomatic efforts in Tehran against mounting physical supply risks, plus caution ahead of the Federal Reserve's Oct 28 rate decision and a firmer US dollar. Talks in Tehran on Monday between Iranian officials and mediators from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan produced agreement to maintain dialogue, but no formal ceasefire or binding agreement to end attacks on maritime corridors. Ship-tracking data cited by DTN put crude exports from the Persian Gulf at approximately 65 percent of pre-conflict levels, down from 90 percent at the start of October, as anti-ship missile threats discourage tanker transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil prices turned positive on Oct 27 after falling about 1 percent earlier in the session, as the chance of talks in Tehran eased fears of a broader Middle East supply shock while renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia highlighted persistent risks, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures were up 40 cents, or 0.4 percent, at $116.24 a barrel by 0718 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 30 cents, or 0.3 percent, at $102.07 a barrel. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday aimed at easing tension in the Middle East, and the four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media said. Last week Brent surged to more than $117 a barrel, the highest since April, after a wave of Iranian attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz, and Brent touched $117 on Monday as well. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data from a Washington-based think tank tracking worldwide maritime security incidents since 2017.

Oil prices fell on Oct 26 after surging last week to near six-month highs, amid hopes of easing hostilities between the United States and Iran, although persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept investors wary, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures were down $1.49, or 1.28 percent, at $115.23 a barrel by 0744 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.76, or 1.7 percent, at $101.51 a barrel. On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said, and top officials from the Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were set to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday. Vandana Hari, founder of Vanda Insights, said concerns over renewed military hostilities had eased that morning but the reprieve may prove temporary, and that volatility was expected to remain elevated with risks still skewed to the upside. The head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, said at an industry event in Singapore on Monday that he does not expect energy markets in 2027 to return to where they were before the Iran war. Reuters also reported that Saudi Aramco will start storing crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, according to the energy ministers of Saudi Arabia and Singapore.

Attacks on commercial vessels continue across the Gulf region, while traffic through the US-facilitated southern route in the Strait of Hormuz is averaging more than 30 transits per day, according to INTERTANKO's latest weekly security update, reported by SAFETY4SEA on Oct 26. Tankers account for approximately 90 percent of these movements. INTERTANKO said no credible evidence had emerged to support Iranian claims that vessels had struck mines laid in regional waters, and questioned Iranian claims concerning the number of ships attacked. In the Red Sea region, INTERTANKO reported that the Houthis have not conducted maritime operations for some time and that renewed attacks against shipping are not expected in the immediate future, although the group retains considerable capabilities to target maritime traffic; Houthi activity is currently focused on fighting Yemen's internationally recognised government and conducting long-range attacks against infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

Gulf countries exported 24.6 million b/d in the week ending Oct 18, surpassing pre-war levels of 23.3 million b/d, according to data compiled by energy analytics firm Kpler and reported on Oct 22. The recovery excludes Iranian exports, which remain constrained by the US blockade, and rests on rerouting: about 40 percent of regional crude exports bypassed the Strait of Hormuz in September, up from 17 percent before the war, with Saudi and UAE pipelines redirecting supplies to Red Sea and Gulf of Oman terminals and more than 70 percent of crude crossing Hormuz in August changing tankers offshore near Fujairah or Sohar. Tanker charter rates and war-risk insurance premiums have surged, making the alternative routes expensive.

Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Oct 23, their highest in nearly six months, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55, or 3.14 percent, their highest since April 29, and US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80, or 3.8 percent. Brent finished the week up 6 percent and West Texas Intermediate ended 2.3 percent higher. Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial, said fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure, and Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, said the market remained concerned about an increase in attacks on tankers even though more oil had recently been transported through the Strait of Hormuz.

In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Oct 22. No volume for the production cut was given in the Reuters reporting. The Libyan loss was cited alongside the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as a support for oil prices on Oct 23.

Oil prices rose over 1 percent on Oct 23 after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures climbed $1.30, or 1.2 percent, to $114.47 a barrel as of 0639 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate rose $1.37, or 1.4 percent, to $100.84. Brent, which settled at its highest since May 4 on Oct 22, was set to close higher for a third successive week. ING analysts said markets are increasingly worried about renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf, that re-escalation seems the most likely path, and that the mere possibility is likely to keep a sizeable geopolitical risk premium embedded in prices even if tensions do not re-escalate.

Brent crude settled at a five-month high on Oct 22, gaining $4.35, or 4.0 percent, to $113.17 a barrel, its highest close since May 4, while US West Texas Intermediate increased $2.32, or 2.4 percent, to $99.47, Reuters reporting via BizFocus said. Analysts at Ritterbusch and Associates attributed the rally to a renewed geopolitical risk premium following another Houthi attack on Saudi infrastructure, and PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and strikes against Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure were outweighing reports of stronger regional crude exports. Morgan Stanley estimated Middle Eastern crude exports reached approximately 17 million b/d last week, against Kpler data showing exports averaged around 18 million b/d in the 12 months before the Iran war.

Oil prices rallied over $2 a barrel on Oct 22 after more Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over a broader escalation, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures climbed $2.82, or 2.59 percent, to $111.64 a barrel at 0626 GMT, close to a five-month high, and US West Texas Intermediate gained $2.24, or 2.31 percent, to $99.39. ING analysts said oil prices remain well bid, with ICE Brent back above $110 a barrel following additional deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia. US crude stocks fell by 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels last week, the US Energy Information Administration said on Oct 21, compared with analysts expectations in a Reuters poll for an 820,000-barrel draw.

Oil prices finished little changed on Oct 21 as prospects for renewed Russia-Ukraine peace talks offset continuing tanker attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and a larger than expected decline in US crude inventories, Reuters reported via OilMonster. Brent crude settled at $108.82 a barrel, up 3 cents, and US West Texas Intermediate settled at $97.15, down 67 cents, after both benchmarks had risen by as much as $2 earlier in the session.

Oil prices gained over $1 on Oct 21, with Brent crude futures up $1.59, or 1.5 percent, to $110.38 a barrel as of 0350 GMT and US West Texas Intermediate up $1.36, or 1.4 percent, to $99.18, Reuters reported. Prices had fallen in the previous session after Iran's president discussed mediation efforts with Pakistan's army chief in Tehran, though Brent had touched a five-month high before easing. DBS head of energy research Suvro Sarkar said the recent sessions reflect profit taking and hopes of a Qatar or Pakistan brokered deal countered by the realisation that any deal is still very distant, compounded by continuing US crude and product inventory drawdowns reported by the American Petroleum Institute (API).

Oil prices advanced on Oct 20, with Brent crude futures up 52 cents, or 0.47 percent, to $110.07 a barrel by 0628 GMT after rising as high as $110.70 in the previous session, the highest since May 20, Reuters reported. The November US West Texas Intermediate contract, set to expire on Oct 20, was up 0.36 percent to $104.03, and the more active December contract rose 26 cents to $98.80. ING analysts said the market is pricing in a significant risk premium and that the premium would erode only if flows continue uninhibited, with no signs of that yet. Kpler said in a note on Monday that at least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks.

Oil prices slipped from a five-month high on Oct 19, with Brent crude futures down $2.29, or 2.08 percent, to $107.57 a barrel by 0619 GMT after settling at the highest since May 19 on Friday, and US West Texas Intermediate at $99.46, down $1.95, Reuters reported. Analysts cited by Reuters said the US waiver on Russia sanctions does little to address the physical supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, where oil tanker attacks continue, and DBS expects oil prices to remain rangebound in the $100 to $110 a barrel range going into the US midterms.

Reuters reported on Oct 17 that Iran has exported some liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and jet fuel since July despite the US naval blockade, concealing cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman. Analysis by United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) showed at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG, estimated at 4.1 million barrels in total, have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July, and a tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September. CENTCOM said on Oct 13 that in the three months of the latest blockade four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships turned around.

Brent touched $110 a barrel on Oct 16 for the first time since May on worries that escalating Middle East tensions could further tighten supplies, while investors assessed how much diesel Russia could supply to the global market, Reuters reported. Brent futures settled $3.94, or 3.7 percent, higher at $109.86, the highest since May 19, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures closed $3.44, or 3.5 percent, higher at $101.41, the highest since September. On the week, Brent rose 4.9 percent and WTI rose 10.4 percent.

Vortexa data reported by Reuters on Oct 13 put Iran's seaborne crude exports at zero through early October, unchanged from the second week of September, when the 14-day average had been 230,000 b/d at the start of that month. Gulf flows excluding Iran rose above 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, led by Saudi exports. Iranian crude on the water fell to 83 million barrels, with 43 million barrels west of Hormuz, and LPG exports fell 48 percent month on month to the lowest since at least January 2023.

Oil rose about 2 percent on Oct 12, with Brent up $2.09 to $106.80 and WTI up $1.93 to $93.78 in Monday morning trade, the highest in nearly two weeks, as weekend tanker and Saudi airport attacks outweighed the announced Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and Russian diesel deal. Gulf oil exports had recovered to 81 percent of prewar levels in September, with crude and condensate at 91 percent but refined products at only 60 percent. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 from $85 and estimated geopolitical risk was adding just over $20 a barrel, while OPEC cut its 2026 demand growth view to 400,000 b/d from 1.4 million b/d at the start of the year.

Treasury officials briefing after the Oct 8 designations said Iran has about 20 million barrels of crude left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, that Tehran has stopped loading and offloading crude under the blockade, and that US forces boarded the sanctioned tanker Davina in the Indian Ocean; Trump said the US is having productive discussions with Iran and will not attack before the Nov 3 midterms.

Saudi Aramco unexpectedly cut its November crude prices for Asian buyers to six-year lows, Reuters reported, while OPEC+ delayed a review that would set members' 2027 output quotas after the Iran war disrupted capacity expansion projects across the Middle East. Two sources told Reuters the delay throws estimates of future production potential into uncertainty.

Iran's rial fell to a new record low on Saturday as the central bank announced an injection of up to $2 billion to support the currency, which has lost more than half its value over the past year under U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade. The free-market dollar traded around 2.688 million rials, up from 2.632 million on Friday, with state banks selling dollars under the central bank's directive.
Iran's seaborne oil exports were 587 million barrels in 2024 (+10.75% y/y); China took 533 million barrels, 91% of the total, up 24% from 2023.
Iran exported 666 million barrels in 2025 (+13.5% y/y), with China by far the largest buyer.

May 2026 exports by sea were just 2.01 million barrels vs 29.7 million in April (-93%); the May total was four Panamax/Handymax naphtha shipments to China plus limited liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Very large crude carrier (VLCC) 2-million-barrel crude shipments dropped to zero.

Iran's pre-war baseline exports were 1.68 million b/d; TankerTrackers estimated they had fallen to zero by early September 2026 and could remain there 'for the foreseeable future' depending on any agreement.

Iran's export stream is medium and heavy sour crude: Iran Light (medium sour, American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity 33.6, 1.46% sulfur) and Iran Heavy (heavy sour, API gravity about 29.5, sulfur about 1.77%), per National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) assays reported by S&P Global Platts.
claims.source: Hellenic Shipping News (citing S&P Global Platts)

claims.text: China's independent refiners buy mainly Iran Light and some Iran Heavy. They crack Iran Light directly in their crude distillation units; Iran Heavy has to be blended with lighter grades first.

Iran Light is a direct substitute for Russian Urals in China's teapot refineries (independent refiners): similar medium sour specs (Iran Light 33.6 API and 1.46% sulfur vs Urals 31.7 API and 1.19%), and teapot sources say Iranian barrels suit their units better than Russian ones.

So the grades hit hardest by a return are medium and heavy sours: Russian Urals first (direct teapot substitute), then the wider medium-sour complex. Light sweets are less exposed, though record ESPO premiums of $20 to $30 per barrel over Brent would also ease.
UANI's 'ghost armada' reached 560 tracked tankers at end-2025 after 83 new vessels were identified during the year; of 180 tankers sanctioned in 2025, 108 had been previously identified by UANI.

China imported ~431 million barrels of Iranian oil in 2023 (over 80% of Iran's exports), rising to ~533 million in 2024 (over 91%), largely via ghost-fleet tankers offloading through intermediaries before reaching China.
claims.source: Claire Jungman, UANI (House Foreign Affairs testimony)

claims.text: Kpler data released on Oct 21 showed total Persian Gulf oil flows reached 24.5 million b/d in the week ending Oct 18, above the 24.4 million b/d average recorded on Feb 22, a week before the war began, Breitbart reported on Oct 24 citing Kpler. The total includes oil shipped through alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, including the Red Sea route and bypass pipelines, and excludes Iran, whose exports have dropped to near zero under the US blockade. Kpler noted ship traffic through the strait itself remains far below pre-war levels, at about 20 known transits over the past ten days against more than 100 ships per day before the war, with many vessels running with transponders off. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Oct 20 that about 400 merchant ships passed through the strait over the preceding week, a far higher estimate than Kpler provided, and Bloomberg reported large tankers traveling in convoys through the strait and transferring oil to other ships after exiting. Vortexa, cited by Bloomberg, put total oil flow lower, at 18 million b/d, only slightly below the pre-war average.

Middle East oil exports have averaged 17.3 million b/d so far in October, up from 16.4 million b/d in September and above the 16.9 million b/d average in the two months before US-Israeli strikes on Iran began on Feb 28, according to Kpler data cited in a Reuters analysis by Ron Bousso on Oct 22. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz hit 11.7 million b/d in October, up from 9.75 million b/d in September and around 82 percent of pre-war levels, helped by ship convoys that sail close to the Omani coastline under US naval protection. Shipping data suggests around a third of crossings continue to use the Iran-controlled northern route. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported 12 attacks in or around Hormuz last week, a record high, and said the actual number was probably much higher because many vessel owners do not report attacks. A supertanker from the Gulf to China is near $1.4 million a day and war risk insurance has climbed to as much as 10 percent of a vessel value in related reporting on the same analysis.

Global shipping costs for oil have surged about sevenfold over the past year because of the war in the Middle East and are likely to remain elevated, according to Goldman Sachs in a note reported by Bloomberg on Oct 21. The average rate for hauling crude has surged above $20 a barrel, up from $3 a year ago, including an extra $7 for the war-risk premium in the Strait of Hormuz and $4 each for higher fuel costs and the impact of ship-to-ship transfers. Goldman said higher freight rates for longer pose some upside risk to its Brent forecast, along with the risks of more intense shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a stickier geopolitical risk premium, with its baseline forecast for Brent a drop to $90 a barrel by year-end.

Attacks on tankers have expanded beyond the Strait of Hormuz, LSEG analysts said in a note cited by Reuters on Oct 21, with Iran targeting vessels as far south as the Gulf of Oman, threatening loadings outside the Arab Gulf as well as the ship to ship transfers that have helped support Middle East loadings as the conflict has dragged on. Ship tracker Kpler said on Oct 19 that at least 18 vessel attacks were recorded over the previous two weeks.

Intensified attacks on commercial vessels cut Gulf crude flows sharply to about 8.5 million b/d on a seven-day average last week from more than 20 million b/d the week before, analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday cited by Reuters on Oct 19. At least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels were reported last week, Kpler added.

Fox News reported that Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which moves roughly 2.6 to 4 million b/d of crude from the Gulf to the Red Sea, could stay largely offline for three to five weeks of repairs after the Oct 4 attack damaged a pumping station at Khurais.

Kpler data reported by CNBC put the seven-day average of crude transiting Hormuz at 13.5 million b/d as of September 28, matching the firm's pre-war baseline for the corridor, while total Middle East Gulf crude shipments including Red Sea outlets ran about 16.5 million b/d in September excluding Iran. The recovery is not a return to normal: over 70 percent of crude crossing the strait changed tankers off Fujairah or Oman in August, refined-product flows through Hormuz remain only about 677,000 b/d versus roughly 3.6 million b/d before the war, and Iran's own crude loadings have effectively hit zero.

War-risk premiums for Saudi-linked tankers loading at Yanbu have risen to about 3% of vessel value from below 1% in early July, while ports further south face quotes as high as 7%, after the London marine insurance market classified the waters as high risk following Houthi attacks near the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The New York Times reported that Iran is conducting roughly 30 drone attacks and 10 missile attacks per week on commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz, a tempo that has turned the strait back into a direct tanker-safety corridor rather than just a congestion problem.

EIA estimated LNG flows through Hormuz fell to 0.8 billion cubic feet per day in the second quarter of 2026, from about 10.5 to 11.4 billion cubic feet per day before the conflict; the agency said its figures supplement vessel tracking with origin, destination and route analysis because AIS signals have become unreliable in the conflict zone.

EIA's quarterly Hormuz series shows the collapse in stages: 20.4 million b/d in Q1 2025, 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 before the war, 14.6 million b/d in Q1 2026 after the February 28 strikes, then 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026. The Q1 2026 split was about 10.7 million b/d of crude and condensate plus 3.9 million b/d of products, down from 14.3 and 6.1 a year earlier.
claims.vintage: Data through Q2 2026; EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook reporting, Aug-Sep 2026

claims.text: EIA figures show Hormuz oil flows fell from 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 to just 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026, while Bab el-Mandeb flows rose from 5.4 to 8.1 million b/d, a major rerouting of the global oil transportation system.

IEA's September 2026 Oil Market Report said more than 10 million b/d of Gulf output remained shut in amid security risks; cumulative supply losses since February exceeded 507 million barrels of observed inventory draws.
claims.vintage: Data through Aug 2026; report Sep 11, 2026; accessed 2026-09-23
claims.source: Namibia Daily News (via Xinhua, citing IEA September OMR)

claims.text: The Baltic VLCC time-charter average rose from ~$198,000/day in July to ~$449,000/day in the first half of September, reaching ~$722,946/day by September 18, 2026, versus ~$79,700/day in mid-September 2025.

TradeWinds reported on Oct 26 that Iran disabled a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz in an incident on Friday, Oct 23, with the report only surfacing days later. TradeWinds said the delayed report from the Friday incident shows a widening time gap between actual incidents and verified reporting. No vessel name, damage assessment or casualty detail was available in the portion of the report open to non-subscribers, so the incident is logged here on the headline facts only.

US President Donald Trump said on Oct 23 that the war with Iran could end quickly, while suggesting that Washington might allow the conflict to gradually wind down, Reuters reported. The comment followed his Oct 22 accusation that Iran was making up fake hits and mines to drive up the price of oil before the US midterm elections, and a rally remark in Fort Myers, Florida on Oct 23 that the US may do another little Epic Fury, the name of the US military campaign against Iran that began on Feb 28, France 24 reported via NewsPlainly.

President Donald Trump accused Iran on Oct 22 of making up fake hits, mines, and everything else to drive up the price of oil before the US midterm elections, and said more oil is coming through the Strait of Hormuz than before the conflict began, the Associated Press reported via SBS News. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had said four tankers were targeted while transferring oil and caught fire, and three others struck naval mines. The Associated Press said the parties' claims were not the same as a confirmed investigation into each vessel, and the number of ships affected, the cause of each incident, and the circumstances of any fires or mine strikes require further verification. No vessel names, flags, or casualty figures were provided in the Iranian statement.

Washington widened its crackdown on Iran's shadow fleet on Oct 21, sanctioning Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm based in Panama and Greece, shipping agents in Singapore and Dubai, and nine vessels, Splash247 reported. The US Treasury said the firm had established corporate structures for shipowners moving hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Iranian oil, liquefied petroleum gas, petrochemicals and steel, and five individuals linked to the practice were also designated. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore was sanctioned for acting as port agent for a shipment of Iranian light crude and providing bunkering services to the shadow fleet tanker Zixuan, and Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line was designated for acting as shipping agent for a company accused of arranging Iranian petrochemical purchases. The action forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August.

The Greek finance ministry said on Oct 22 that it was implementing sanctions in place linked to Iran and backed efforts to effectively combat money laundering and the financing of terrorism, Reuters reported. The statement came after the US Treasury Department said on Oct 21 that it imposed sanctions on Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm based in Greece and Panama, and that the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued an administrative subpoena to advance an investigation into a Greek bank, which it did not name. The ministry said all available information is being evaluated and appropriate measures are being taken in accordance with established procedures and applicable national, European Union, and international law.

Iran told Pakistan's army chief there would be no talks with Washington until its demands were met, Iranian media outlet Nournews reported on Oct 20, adding that a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran; there was no official confirmation of the reports. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Oct 20 that Iran has not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthis to its offer to help broker peace talks. The death toll from the Oct 19 Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces rose to 73 as fighting intensified, Reuters reported on Oct 21, up from 58 reported on Oct 20.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct 19 they launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport, Reuters reported on Oct 20. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. No damage or disruption to Saudi oil operations has been confirmed from these claims.

The death toll from the Oct 19 Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province was updated to 58 people killed with more than 200 injured, Reuters reported on Oct 20, up from the 18 killed reported in early coverage on Oct 19. The camp attack came as government forces press a campaign to recapture areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

At least 18 people were killed on Oct 19 in an attack by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, four government and medical sources told Reuters. The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise in Shabwa, an energy-rich coastal province in south-central Yemen. Government forces this month began a campaign aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea, while the group besieges Taiz.

The UN Security Council issued a presidential statement on Oct 16 condemning in the strongest terms the Houthis' continued and escalatory attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy facilities, and their continued attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, affirming Saudi Arabia's inherent right of self-defence. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry welcomed the statement on Oct 17, and Riyadh blamed Iran for encouraging the escalation.

Two missiles landed within the perimeter of Aden International Airport on Oct 16, about 500 metres from a Yemenia Airways flight preparing for takeoff to Cairo and about 100 metres from the centre of the runway, with no one killed, Yemeni officials said. The Saudi-led coalition said on Oct 16 it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu, the Red Sea terminus of the East-West pipeline, two cruise missiles over the Red Sea, and three drones in the southern and Riyadh regions. Iran on Oct 16 denied Saudi accusations that Tehran encouraged the Houthi escalation and offered to mediate.

A senior Iranian commander, Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, said on Oct 15 that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and any vessel passage must be coordinated with Iran's armed forces, warning that uncoordinated transits would face consequences. He said the IRGC Navy holds the western side of the strait while the regular army operates on the eastern side into the Sea of Oman.

A container ship and a dry bulk carrier sank near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours, maritime officials said on Oct 14, the second and third vessels sunk since the war began on Feb 28, according to IMO casualty data. The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank weeks after a Sep 23 projectile strike that killed one crew member; the rest were evacuated at the time.

The Houthis hit an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Dhahran on Oct 14, causing a limited fire, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said. The strike extends a week of Houthi missile and drone fire at Saudi targets, including four hits on Riyadh's international airport, with a strike on Saturday killing 13 people.

Iran's IRGC Navy claimed on Oct 11 that a 'violating' crude supertanker exploded after striking a naval mine while attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an 'unauthorized route' with its navigation systems switched off, and warned such vessels would be treated as hostile. No vessel name, flag, or independent confirmation was provided; UKMTO logged the same window's strike only as an unknown projectile hit with crew safe.

A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Oct 10 killed 12 people and wounded 309, per Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority, the deadliest such attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade; a fresh strike Oct 11 killed one and injured 11. US President Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, while Saudi Arabia intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile headed for Khamis Mushait on Oct 12.

Iran's IRGC Navy claimed it struck the LPG carrier NV Sunshine south of the Strait of Hormuz for using an 'illegal route,' saying the engine room caught fire; the vessel's owner told AAP the tanker was not attacked, is operating normally, and all crew are safe.

The Houthis hit Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport with two cruise missiles on Thursday, killing three Saudi nationals and injuring several; Europe's EASA widened its Saudi airspace advisory on Friday, OPSGROUP advised members to avoid Saudi Arabia, and airlines including Lufthansa, Etihad and flydubai cancelled Riyadh flights, with 131 cancellations by Friday afternoon per Flightradar24.

Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran war began on February 28, with at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers in the week of September 28 to October 5, according to three maritime security sources; the UN's International Maritime Organization logged nine incidents for the same week.

UKMTO reported that a tanker was struck by multiple projectiles 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, with casualties reported and authorities investigating; it is the first reported attack that deep inside the Persian Gulf since a tanker was hit southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, on September 9.

Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden's international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early Wednesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a separate Houthi ballistic missile launched toward the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.

Three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on two Saudi airports, the kingdom's civil aviation authorities said: one killed and eight wounded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and two killed and 28 wounded at Abha airport. The Saudi-led coalition vowed retaliation and said it had attacked more than 80 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib.

IRGC commander-in-chief's adviser Mohammadreza Naqdi told Fars News Agency that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and under full control of Iran's armed forces until Iran's demands are met, and said Iran will soon block the remaining routes hugging Oman's coast; US Central Command on Oct 7 publicly rejected the claim as false, saying traffic was flowing with about 20 million barrels of crude moving through. Provisional Kpler data put regional crude exports at a seven-day moving average of 18.3 million b/d on September 30, topping pre-war levels on 14 days in September.

Since the war began in late February, 93 ships have been hit and 24 seafarers killed, Splash247 reported; the shrinking pool of willing crews is pushing tanker captain pay as high as $100,000 a month plus $50,000 per Hormuz transit, with war-risk insurance for single tanker voyages climbing to $20 million and some tanker earnings nearing $1.3 million a day.

Twelve seafarers were injured when the 114,600-dwt LR2 tanker On Peace was struck by a projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz; UKMTO confirmed the incident and the wounded were hospitalised in Khasab, Oman, on Oct 6.

Yemen's Houthis claimed three operations on Oct 6 using ballistic and cruise missiles plus drones, targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, and military sites across southern Saudi Arabia, and warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace; Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.

Saudi naval forces struck military targets in the Houthi-held Red Sea port of Hodeidah, destroying weapons depots and facilities holding booby-trapped boats and naval mines, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said, adding that the operation prevented a planned attack on shipping routes in the southern Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline was halted again on Oct 4 after a fresh attack damaged a pumping station at Khurais, east of Riyadh, a source in the kingdom's energy sector told Agence France-Presse. The source said the Khurais station had not been targeted before and the damage was extensive; Kpler data cited in the report shows the line's flows had already been halted from Sep 11 to Sep 22, and the pipeline has become essential to Saudi exports since the Hormuz blockade cut the main route.

UKMTO issued four warnings and an advisory on Oct 5 as attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz intensified, including a projectile strike that set a ship's engine room on fire with the crew still fighting it and no casualties reported. UKMTO also logged Iranian forces hailing the Liberia-registered tanker Singapore Energy 11 nm north of Oman with a warning it would be fired upon unless it turned back, plus time-late reports of Oct 3-4 strikes on an LPG tanker and two crude tankers, bringing its October count to nine reports.

A Bangladeshi national, Md Sajib Hossain of Cumilla, was killed on Oct 4 when a Houthi missile or drone struck a Saudi Aramco facility at Al Khurais, according to a Bangladesh foreign ministry press release issued Oct 5. The ministry condemned the attack and said its Riyadh embassy is coordinating with Saudi authorities to repatriate the body; it is the first independently reported casualty from the Oct 4 Houthi strikes on Aramco sites, which Saudi Arabia itself has still not commented on.

Oil prices rose on October 4 after the Houthis said they fired ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area, in retaliation for about 50 Saudi-led strikes in Yemen that Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. Brent crude futures rose 81 cents to $103.06 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained 46 cents to $91.57 a barrel.

UKMTO logged five incidents on Oct 5 in and near the Strait of Hormuz: four tanker attacks, including delayed reports of an Oct 4 strike on an inbound LPG tanker and another on a crude oil tanker, plus an inbound tanker hailed by IRGC forces off Khasab, Oman, and ordered to turn back or risk being targeted; the tanker complied.

President Trump said on Oct 6 he was 'always open' to direct talks with Iran, even as UKMTO logged a ninth ship attack in the region within a week; the remarks followed a reported Camp David meeting where Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Rubio discussed next steps in the Iran war.

Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Oct 4 that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions from a June interim agreement with the US are met, adding that Washington must understand the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over. The statement followed Tehran's receipt, via Qatari mediators, of the US reply to its UN General Assembly proposal for a seven-day reopening; the Foreign Ministry stressed its current focus is Hormuz security, not nuclear talks, and denied offering IAEA inspections for sanctions relief.

Fighting centered on Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, with the Houthis reporting 55 of their fighters killed on Oct 2 while government sources told AFP 26 troops had died; Saudi authorities separately reported a Houthi projectile damaged a school in the border city of Najran.

The physical oil market is pricing a far tighter situation than futures: Europe's Dated Brent benchmark jumped above $120 per barrel even as ICE Brent sat near $101, a divergence the report ties to droned tankers in Hormuz, the European diesel release, and China's reinstated refined-product export ban.

Iran's Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned for personal reasons and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted the resignation, state media said on October 4. Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the government-owned National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), was named acting minister. Paknejad had held the post since August 2024 and departs seven months into the US-Iran war, which has squeezed Iran's economy and oil exports.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported that Houthi forces captured the key supply route between the cities of Taiz and Aden on October 4, part of their campaign to seize Taiz City. Yemen's government announced an offensive across all fronts against the Houthis, but ISW's Critical Threats Project had not yet observed any offensive action. The loss of government-held ground narrows the protected corridor around the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb approach.
claims.source: Institute for the Study of War

claims.text: Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi announced the start of a major military operation to retake Houthi-held territory, with Saudi Arabia leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground; the announcement followed weeks of preparations aimed at reversing the Houthis' seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The US Treasury designated the Kremlin-linked A7 financial network a 'significant transnational criminal organization,' saying its subagents disguised payments involving sanctioned entities as legitimate commercial transactions to help Russian and Iranian entities move money outside the banking system, including for Iranian oil sales and weapons procurement. FinCEN said A7 subagents processed more than $17 billion between January 2025 and June 2026. A7 denied any Iran links on October 2.

The U.S. is sending roughly 9,000 troops aboard ships to the Middle East, including the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious group, potentially putting three carrier groups in the region. President Trump told Time it is possible he ramps up bombing of Iran after the Nov 3 elections, and said Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz in its latest ceasefire proposal, which he rejected as not good enough.

Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive to push the Houthis off the Bab el-Mandeb strait, citing six Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats; Riyadh is weighing either a focused coastal assault or a broader multi-front campaign in Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf that could mobilize more than 100,000 Yemeni troops, with timing estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said a crude tanker was struck by an unknown projectile on October 3 about four nautical miles east of Oman, and a second tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on October 4 with damage to its engine room. Crews were reported safe and no environmental damage was recorded. Separately, Iran's parliament speaker said the strait will not fully reopen until seven conditions under the Islamabad Memorandum are met.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group struck an Aramco oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones late on Oct 3, sparking fires, and an AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters battling a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery south of the capital; the Houthis also said Saudi Arabia launched 94 strikes on Houthi-held areas in the preceding 24 hours.

G7 leaders agreed Oct 2 to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves over four months via the IEA, starting immediately, with substantial diesel in the first 20 days and further diesel releases under discussion. The joint statement also called for restoring navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Five Indian nationals aboard the struck Kuwait-flagged VLCC Kazimah III were brought ashore in Oman after the Embassy of India in Oman coordinated the rescue, with Omani authorities assisting. India says more than 4,500 Indian seafarers are currently on commercial vessels in the region.

Iranian outlets reported a supertanker able to carry 2.5 million barrels was hit about 8 kilometers off the Omani coast while sailing what Iran's Fars News Agency called an 'unauthorized route' south of the strait, and caught fire. UKMTO confirmed it had received a report of a tanker incident; the vessel's identity and the Fars account were not independently corroborated.

Three tankers were hit by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on September 29, according to time-late reports received by UKMTO: the Liberia-flagged, AIS-dark VLCC Mersin Prosperity, the Aframax Sinbad and the products tanker Al Ruwais, identified by shipping intelligence firm Marisks (carried by Reuters). A separate September 28 strike on a tanker caused a fire that has since been extinguished, with the vessel underway and crew safe.

Bab el-Mandeb traffic fell to 11 commodity-vessel transits on September 27, the lowest in months, after Houthi strikes on Saudi coastal installations; on September 25 the Houthis captured Mayun island at the Red Sea entrance, a key position over the alternative lane for Saudi oil while Hormuz is disrupted.

Diplomacy stalled: President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz reopening proposal on September 26, and the Wall Street Journal reported US officials expect airstrikes to resume after the November midterms.
claims.source: Seoul Economic Daily (citing AFP/Reuters); Wall Street Journal

claims.text: The recovery split widened: Kpler's September snapshot put regional exports at 12.8 million b/d (highest since February), Hormuz at ~7.4 million b/d and Saudi Arabia at ~5.4 million b/d versus 2.4 million in August, while Iranian crude exports stayed at zero for 60+ days.

The Kuwait Oil Tanker Co VLCC Al Funtas, struck by a suspected projectile north of Khasab on September 28, had its onboard fire extinguished, all crew safe and no environmental impact reported, with the vessel remaining underway toward a port of refuge rather than becoming disabled inside the chokepoint.

UKMTO said three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles in separate attacks on September 29: one crude carrier struck on the port side, one tanker transiting inbound, and one LNG carrier, bringing the total to four vessels hit since the Al Funtas VLCC was struck, according to verified sources cited by TradeWinds and corroborated by UKMTO-sourced reports.
